title: Setting the Wheel in Motion
bigQuestion: Why do Buddhists treat one short talk to five listeners as the start of their whole tradition?

story.title: The Five Who Meant to Ignore Him
story.kicker: Five men agree to give their old companion no welcome, and then find they cannot keep their promise.
paragraphs: The later tradition tells the scene this way. Five wandering ascetics are living in a deer park at Isipatana, near Varanasi. Once they practiced hard fasting with a man named Gotama. Then he gave up fasting and ate a meal. The five decided he had quit, and they left him.

Now they see him walking toward them. They agree among themselves not to stand, not to take his bowl and not to greet him. They will only set out a seat, since he was once of good family. In the Vinaya's telling, their plan falls apart as he comes near. One takes his bowl, one sets out water and one prepares a seat.

At first they still call him by his name and speak to him as an equal. The Buddha, as the text presents him, tells them not to address him that way. He says he has found what they were looking for. They doubt him. He asks whether he has ever spoken like this before. They admit he has not, and they agree to listen.

What he says next is the talk Buddhists call the first sermon, the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Dhamma. Buddhists in every school recite it. Theravada Buddhists remember it each year on Asalha Puja. This chapter reads it closely, line by line, in the 1881 translation by T.W. Rhys Davids.
story.think: Why might a tradition keep the detail that the first listeners planned to ignore the speaker?

lessons.title: Where and to Whom
lessons.mainIdea: The first sermon is set in a deer park near Varanasi and is spoken to five former companions of the Buddha.
reading: Every sutta opens by saying where it happened and who was there. The first sermon names the deer park at Isipatana, today called Sarnath, near the city of Varanasi. It names the listeners as the group of five monks. The Pali name of the talk is *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*, the discourse on setting the wheel of the Dhamma in motion.

The sutta appears in the Samyutta Nikaya, at 56.11, in the collection of talks on the truths. A longer version, with the story of the journey to Sarnath, appears in the Vinaya, in the book called the Mahavagga. Rhys Davids translated the sutta in Sacred Books of the East volume 11 in 1881. That English version is now in the public domain.

Scholars date the Buddha's life to about the fifth century BCE, often c. 480 to c. 400 BCE. Theravada tradition gives earlier dates, placing his death in 544 or 543 BCE. The words were passed down by memory for centuries. They were written down in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE, as Sri Lankan chronicles report. So the text we read is the *sutta* as its reciters kept it, not a recording.

words.d: the Pali name of the first sermon: the discourse on setting the wheel of the Dhamma in motion
a discourse or talk of the Buddha as the Pali Canon records it; sutra in Sanskrit
the Connected Discourses, a collection in the Pali Canon that groups talks by topic

look.title: Dating the Buddha
rows: Written down in Sri Lanka, c. (BCE)
look.cite: Common scholarly and traditional dates; see Richard Gombrich and Heinz Bechert's work on the Buddha's dates
look.prompt: About how many years separate the traditional death date from the time the texts were written down?

check.q: Where is the first sermon set?
choices: In the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi
Under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya
Between two sal trees at Kusinara
check.why: The sutta names the deer park at Isipatana (Sarnath) near Varanasi. The Bodhi tree is where Buddhists say he awakened.

check.q: Where in the Pali Canon is the first sermon found?
check.why: The sutta is Samyutta Nikaya 56.11. Digha Nikaya 16 is the account of the Buddha's last days.

check.q: How were the words of the sermon kept before they were written down?
choices: On stone pillars from the start
On palm leaves copied in the Buddha's lifetime
check.why: The Pali texts were passed down orally and, as Sri Lankan chronicles report, written down in the first century BCE.

lessons.title: The Two Extremes
lessons.mainIdea: The sermon opens by naming two extremes a person who has left home should avoid.
reading: The sermon does not begin with the truths. It begins with a warning. Rhys Davids renders the opening this way: there are two extremes which one who has given up the world ought to avoid. The first is a life given to pleasures, which the text calls low and unprofitable. The second is a life given to self-torment, which the text calls painful and unprofitable.

The listeners knew the second extreme well. They had fasted with Gotama for years. The sermon's first move, then, speaks to their own past. It tells them that the hard path they admired did not lead where they hoped. Readers often point out that the Buddha, as the text presents him, had tried both extremes himself: a palace life and harsh fasting.

Between the two, the sutta says, lies a middle path. It says this path opens the eyes, gives understanding, and leads to peace, insight and *nibbana*. Buddhists across schools call their way the *Middle Way* for this reason. The phrase later took on other meanings too, as when Mahayana thinkers spoke of a middle between being and non-being.

words.d: the path the first sermon places between a life of pleasure and a life of self-torment
Pali for nirvana: the ending of craving and suffering, the goal Buddhists describe
a person who gives up comfort, such as food or sleep, as a religious practice

look.title: The Opening Line
look.text: There are two extremes, O Bhikkhus, which he who has given up the world, ought to avoid.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta 2, tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881)
look.prompt: Who is being addressed here, and why would this opening matter to them in particular?

check.q: What are the two extremes the sermon names?
choices: A life of pleasure and a life of self-torment
check.why: The sutta names devotion to pleasures and devotion to self-mortification as the two extremes.

check.q: Why would the second extreme speak directly to the five listeners?
choices: They had practiced harsh fasting with Gotama
They were princes living in luxury
They had never met him before
check.why: The Vinaya story says the five had fasted with him and left when he ate.

check.q: What does the sermon say lies between the two extremes?
check.why: The sutta calls the path between the extremes the middle path, which Buddhists call the Middle Way.

lessons.title: Reading a Spoken Text
lessons.mainIdea: Repetition and numbered lists in the suttas come from a tradition of memory and recitation.
reading: Read the sermon aloud and you notice repetition. Phrases return again and again with one word changed. Each truth is stated, then stated again in the same frame. To a silent reader today this can feel slow. To a monk reciting with others, it was a way to keep every word exact.

The suttas also love numbered lists: two extremes, four truths, an eightfold path, three turnings, twelve aspects. Scholars such as Rupert Gethin note that lists work like hooks for memory. A reciter who knows there are eight parts will notice if one is missing. Buddhist teachers today still teach through these lists.

So a close reader asks two questions. What does the passage say? And how does its shape help it survive? The sermon's repetition is not padding. It is how an *oral tradition* guarded the text for centuries before it was written. It is also why the sutta still works well when chanted, as monks do at Asalha Puja.

words.d: teachings passed on by speaking and memory rather than in writing
saying a text aloud from memory, often together with others
a Theravada holy day in July that remembers the first sermon

look.title: The Sermon's Lists
look.prompt: How would knowing these counts help a monk reciting the text from memory?

check.q: Why do scholars think the suttas repeat phrases so often?
choices: Scribes were paid by the page
The Buddha forgot what he said
Repetition helped reciters keep the text exact
check.why: The texts were kept by oral recitation, and repetition protects memory.

check.q: How many aspects result from four truths each turned three times?
check.why: Four truths times three turnings gives twelve aspects, which the sutta itself counts.

check.q: What is Asalha Puja?
choices: A Theravada day that remembers the first sermon
The festival of the Buddha's birth in Japan
A day for Jataka plays only
check.why: Theravada Buddhists mark the first sermon on Asalha Puja, the full moon of the month Asalha.

sections.title: The Four Truths, Line by Line

lessons.title: The Truth of Suffering
lessons.mainIdea: The first truth names dukkha, the unsatisfactory side of life, through a list of human experiences.
reading: Rhys Davids renders the first truth as the noble truth concerning suffering. The sutta then lists what it means. Birth is suffering. Decay is suffering. Illness and death are suffering. Union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant are suffering. Not getting what one wishes is suffering.

The Pali word is *dukkha*. Many translators now say that suffering is too narrow. Dukkha can also mean stress, unease or unsatisfactoriness. Walpola Rahula argued in 1959 that no single English word covers it. The list in the sutta ranges from great pain, like death, to ordinary frustration, like wanting something and not getting it.

Buddhist teachers stress that this truth is a diagnosis, not a complaint. Many compare the four truths to a doctor's method: name the illness, its cause, its cure and the treatment. The sutta itself does not use the doctor image. Later commentators and modern teachers do. Readers should keep the text and its later readings apart.

words.d: suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness; the subject of the first noble truth
one of the four statements in the first sermon: suffering, its cause, its ending and the path
naming what is wrong and why, as a doctor does

look.title: The First Truth Stated
look.text: Now this, O Bhikkhus, is the noble truth concerning suffering.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta 5, tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881)
look.prompt: Rhys Davids chose 'suffering' for dukkha. What might a reader miss if they take that word only as great pain?

check.q: Which Pali word does the first truth name?
check.why: The first truth concerns dukkha. Tanha is craving, the subject of the second truth.

check.q: Why do many translators think 'suffering' is too narrow for dukkha?
choices: Dukkha also covers stress and dissatisfaction
check.why: Translators such as Rahula note that dukkha ranges from pain to plain unsatisfactoriness.

check.q: Where does the comparison of the four truths to a doctor's method come from?
choices: The opening line of the sutta
check.why: The sutta does not use the doctor image; later Buddhist readers do.

lessons.title: The Cause: Craving
lessons.mainIdea: The second truth names tanha, craving or thirst, as the origin of suffering.
reading: The second truth, in the sutta's words, concerns the origin of suffering. The Pali word is *tanha*, literally thirst. Rhys Davids renders it as craving. The text names three kinds: craving for sense pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

The image of thirst is worth pausing on. Thirst returns after it is satisfied. The sutta describes craving as leading to renewed becoming and delighting now here, now there. Theravada teachers read this as a claim about how karma and rebirth continue. Some modern readers focus instead on how craving shapes a single day.

Notice what the sutta does not name as the cause. It does not blame the world, the body or other people. It points to a pattern of wanting inside experience. Buddhists believe this is why the problem can be addressed: if craving is the cause, then its ending is possible. That idea leads straight to the third truth.

words.d: craving or thirst; the origin of suffering in the second noble truth
the Buddhist teaching that beings are born again according to their karma
intentional action and its results; kamma in Pali

look.title: Three Kinds of Thirst
look.text: The sutta lists craving for sense pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. The first is wanting pleasant things. The second is wanting to be or to become something. The third is wanting something to stop or disappear.
look.prompt: Why might the text count wanting something to end as craving too? Explain with an everyday example.

check.q: What does tanha literally mean?
check.why: Tanha means thirst; translators render it craving.

check.q: Which is one of the three kinds of craving the sutta names?
check.why: The sutta names craving for sense pleasures, for existence and for non-existence.

check.q: What does the second truth name as the origin of suffering?
check.why: The second truth locates the origin of suffering in craving, not in the world or others.

lessons.title: The End and the Path
lessons.mainIdea: The third truth names the ending of craving, and the fourth names the eightfold path that leads there.
reading: The third truth concerns the cessation of suffering. The sutta describes it as the complete fading away and ending of that very craving, letting it go and being free of it. Buddhists call this state *nibbana* in Pali, nirvana in Sanskrit. The word suggests a flame going out.

The fourth truth names the path. The sutta lists eight parts: right views, right aspirations, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right rapture, in Rhys Davids' wording. Modern translators often render the last as right concentration. Buddhist teachers group the eight into wisdom, ethics and meditation.

The word right translates samma, which can also mean complete or whole. So the path is not a checklist done in order. Teachers describe the eight as supporting one another, like strands in a rope. Here the sermon returns to its start: this *Noble Eightfold Path* is the middle path it named at the opening.

words.d: ending or stopping; the subject of the third noble truth
the eight parts of the way to the end of suffering in the fourth truth
the Pali word translated right; it can also mean complete or whole

look.title: Two Translations of One Step
look.text: Rhys Davids (1881) renders the eighth step 'right rapture.' Many modern translators render the same Pali word, samadhi, as 'right concentration.' One stresses a joyful state; the other stresses steady focus.
look.prompt: How could a translator's word choice change what a reader thinks the path asks for?

check.q: What does the third truth describe?
choices: The eight steps of the path
The ending of craving and suffering
check.why: The third truth is cessation, the fading and ending of craving.

check.q: How do Buddhist teachers commonly group the eight parts of the path?
check.why: The eight parts are commonly grouped as wisdom, ethics (sila) and meditation (samadhi).

check.q: What does the Pali word samma, translated 'right,' can also mean?
check.why: Samma carries the sense of complete or whole, which is why teachers describe the parts as working together.

lessons.title: Three Turnings of Each Truth
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta says each truth was known in three ways, making twelve aspects in all.
reading: After naming the four truths, the sutta has the Buddha describe his own knowledge. For each truth, he says, there were three stages. First: this is the truth. Second: this truth is to be done in a certain way. Third: this has been done. Readers call these the three turnings or three phases.

Each truth has its own task. Suffering is to be fully understood. Craving is to be abandoned. Cessation is to be realized. The path is to be developed. So the four truths are not only facts to know. As the sutta frames them, each asks for a different response.

The Buddha, as the text presents him, then says that until this knowledge in twelve aspects was complete, he did not claim full awakening. Once it was, he did. Buddhist commentators read this passage as the heart of the sermon. It shows the truths as a practice, not only a teaching.

words.d: the three ways each truth is known in the sermon: what it is, what is to be done, and that it has been done
the Buddha's full understanding as Buddhists describe it; often translated enlightenment
in Buddhist texts, to know directly for oneself, not only to hear about

look.title: Four Truths, Four Tasks
look.text: Suffering: to be fully understood. Its origin, craving: to be abandoned. Its cessation: to be realized. The path: to be developed. The sutta pairs each truth with a verb.
look.prompt: Why might a teacher pair each truth with a different action rather than one action for all four?

check.q: What task does the sutta pair with the truth of craving?
check.why: Craving is to be abandoned; the path is to be developed; cessation is to be realized.

check.q: When, according to the sutta, did the Buddha claim full awakening?
choices: After his knowledge in all twelve aspects was complete
check.why: The sutta says he did not claim awakening until the twelve aspects were complete.

check.q: What task goes with the fourth truth, the path?
check.why: The path is to be developed, or cultivated, as the sutta frames it.

lessons.title: Kondanna Understands
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta ends by saying one listener, Kondanna, understood, and tradition counts him as the first to do so.
reading: At the end of the talk, the sutta turns to the listeners. It says that the eye of truth arose in Kondanna, one of the five. What arose was the insight that whatever has the nature to arise also has the nature to cease. It is a short line, but Buddhists treat it as a turning point.

The Buddha, in the text, exclaims that Kondanna has understood. From this, the text says, Kondanna gained the name Annata Kondanna, Kondanna who knows. Theravada tradition counts him as the first person to enter the path through the Buddha's teaching. In the Vinaya's fuller story, he then asks to be ordained, and the *sangha* begins.

Notice the content of his insight. It is not a new fact about the four truths. It is a general pattern: what begins, ends. Theravada commentators call this the stream entry of the first disciple. Later the other four understand too, over the following days, after more teaching.

words.d: one of the five listeners; the sutta says he was the first to understand the teaching
the community of Buddhist monks and nuns, or more widely of all Buddhists
in Theravada teaching, the first stage of the path toward awakening

look.title: A One-Line Insight
look.text: The sutta sums up Kondanna's understanding in one idea: whatever is subject to arising is subject to ceasing. It does not repeat the four truths. It gives a pattern.
look.prompt: How might this one pattern connect to each of the four truths? Pick one truth and explain.

check.q: Who does the sutta say understood first?
check.why: The sutta names Kondanna. Ananda was the Buddha's attendant later in his life.

check.q: What did Kondanna understand, as the text puts it?
check.why: The eye of truth arose: whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease.

check.q: What does the name Annata Kondanna mean?
check.why: The Buddha's exclamation gave him the name Annata Kondanna, Kondanna who has understood.

lessons.title: The Cry Through the Worlds
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta ends with gods proclaiming the event from world to world, a sign of how its tellers valued it.
reading: The sermon does not end with the five. The text says that earth-dwelling gods raised a cry: the wheel of the Dhamma has been set in motion at Benares, and no one in the world can turn it back. The cry passes up through heaven after heaven, each group of gods repeating it, until it reaches the Brahma world.

The sutta then says the ten-thousand-fold world system shook and a great light appeared. Here the text uses the language of cosmology, the Buddhist picture of many worlds and many kinds of beings. Buddhists have read the passage in several ways. Many traditional readers take it as an account of events. Some modern readers read it as a way of saying the event was cosmic in importance.

A careful student does not need to decide. The task is to describe what the text says and why its tellers included it. The repeating cry uses the same memory technique as the rest of the sutta. It also gives the talk its name: the *Dhamma* has begun to turn, like a wheel that has started rolling.

words.d: the Buddha's teaching, and the truth it points to; dharma in Sanskrit
a picture of how the universe is arranged, with its worlds and beings
in Buddhist cosmology, a high heavenly realm of the god Brahma and similar beings

look.title: The Gods' Cry
look.text: The sutta says the gods of the earth cried out that the supreme wheel of the Dhamma had been set rolling by the Blessed One at Benares, and that no ascetic, brahmin, god, Mara or Brahma could turn it back. The cry rose from heaven to heaven.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta 25-28, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11; paraphrased from tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: Why might a teller want the whole universe to hear what five men heard in a deer park?

check.q: What do the gods proclaim at the end of the sutta?
choices: The wheel of the Dhamma has been set in motion
check.why: The gods cry that the wheel of the Dhamma has been set rolling at Benares.

check.q: Which is a fair description of how Buddhists read the cry through the worlds?
choices: Some take it as events, some as a sign of the sermon's importance
It is a later English addition
It is found only in Zen texts
check.why: Readers differ: many traditional readers take it as an account, some modern readers read it as expressing significance.

check.q: What gives the sutta its name?
choices: The image of the Dhamma as a wheel set rolling
check.why: Dhammacakkappavattana means setting in motion the wheel of the Dhamma.

lessons.title: The Three Jewels Complete
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists call it the first sermon because, as tradition tells it, the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha were all present for the first time.
reading: Buddhists speak of the Three Jewels or Three Refuges: the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. Before the sermon, the tradition says, there was a Buddha but no community that followed his teaching. After it, the five became the first monks. So Buddhist teachers often say the Three Jewels were complete for the first time at Sarnath.

This is one reason Buddhists call it the first sermon, even though the tradition reports that the Buddha had spoken with others before. Two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, offered him food earlier and took refuge. But they received no teaching of the truths. The sermon at Sarnath is the first teaching of the Dhamma as a path.

For this reason Sarnath became a place of pilgrimage. The emperor Ashoka set up a pillar there in the third century BCE. Its lion capital is now the national emblem of India. The wheel on the Indian flag also recalls the wheel of Dhamma, a sign of how widely the image traveled.

words.d: the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha; also called the Three Refuges
a place of safety; Buddhists say they take refuge in the Three Jewels
a journey to a holy place for religious reasons

look.title: Before and After Sarnath
look.text: Before: a Buddha, as tradition says, and two merchants who offered food. After: a Buddha, a teaching stated in order, and five monks who follow it. Buddhists mark the change with the phrase 'the Three Jewels complete.'
look.prompt: Why might a community date its beginning from the first teaching rather than the founder's awakening?

check.q: What are the Three Jewels?
choices: The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha
check.why: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, the Three Jewels.

check.q: Why did the two merchants not count as hearers of the first sermon?
choices: They offered food but received no teaching of the truths
check.why: Tradition says Tapussa and Bhallika gave food and took refuge before any teaching of the truths.

check.q: Which ruler set up a pillar at Sarnath in the third century BCE?
check.why: Ashoka's pillar at Sarnath has the lion capital now used as India's emblem.

lessons.title: One Sermon, Many Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada, Mahayana and modern readers all honor the first sermon but read its place differently.
reading: Theravada Buddhists treat the first sermon as a foundation. It is chanted at ordinations and at Asalha Puja. Monks in Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar learn it by heart. For Theravada teachers, the four truths and eightfold path are the core of the whole Dhamma.

Many Mahayana traditions honor it too, but some describe it as the first turning of the wheel. Some Mahayana sutras speak of a second turning, the teaching of emptiness, and a third turning, the teaching found in texts such as the Samdhinirmocana Sutra. In that view the first sermon is true and needed, but not the last word.

Modern readers add their own emphases. Some present the four truths as practical psychology. Others, such as Thich Nhat Hanh in The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching (1998), focus on transforming suffering in daily life. Scholars ask how the text grew over time. A careful reader describes each view without ranking them.

words.d: the Way of the Elders; the Buddhist school of Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia, using the Pali Canon
the Great Vehicle; Buddhist traditions of East Asia and Tibet that center the bodhisattva path
a Mahayana scheme that calls the first sermon the first of three stages of teaching

look.title: First Turning or Foundation?
look.text: A Theravada monk says: the four truths are the whole teaching in brief. A Tibetan teacher says: the four truths are the first turning, and later turnings open further. Both honor the same sermon.
look.prompt: How can both readers respect the text while giving it a different place? Answer without deciding who is right.

check.q: How do some Mahayana traditions describe the first sermon?
choices: As the first of three turnings of the wheel
check.why: Some Mahayana texts speak of three turnings, with the first sermon as the first.

check.q: Where is the first sermon chanted in Theravada practice?
choices: Never; it is only read silently
At ordinations and on Asalha Puja
check.why: Theravada monks chant it at ordinations and on Asalha Puja.

check.q: What is the fairest way to describe how different Buddhists read the sermon?
choices: All honor it, but place it differently
Only one school knows about it
Modern readers have replaced older views
check.why: Theravada, Mahayana and modern readers honor it while giving it different roles.

lessons.title: Key Terms in Context
lessons.mainIdea: The terms dukkha, tanha and nibbana form a chain in the sermon: the problem, its cause and its ending.
reading: Three Pali words carry the sermon's argument. *Dukkha* names the problem. *Tanha* names its cause. *Nibbana* names its ending. The fourth truth, the path, names how to get from one to the other. Seen this way, the four truths make one chain of reasoning.

Each word is hard to translate. Dukkha can be suffering or unease. Tanha can be craving or thirst. Nibbana can be blowing out, as of a flame, or release. Translators choose, and each choice shapes a reader's picture. That is why a close reader keeps the Pali word in view beside the English.

Spelling also varies. Pali forms are dukkha, kamma, nibbana and dhamma. Sanskrit forms are duhkha, karma, nirvana and dharma. English books use both. Theravada writers tend to use Pali; many Mahayana writers use Sanskrit. Neither spelling is more correct. They point to the same terms in two languages of Buddhist texts.

words.d: suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness; Sanskrit duhkha
craving or thirst; Sanskrit trishna
the ending of craving and suffering; Sanskrit nirvana
the language of the Theravada scriptures

look.title: A Chain of Four
look.text: Problem: dukkha. Cause: tanha. Ending: nibbana. Way: the eightfold path. The sermon states them in that order, and each step depends on the one before.
look.prompt: Explain in two sentences why the third truth depends on the second.

check.q: What is the Sanskrit form of the Pali word nibbana?
check.why: Nibbana (Pali) and nirvana (Sanskrit) are the same term.

check.q: In the sermon's chain, what does tanha name?
check.why: Tanha, craving, is named in the second truth as the origin of suffering.

check.q: Why do close readers keep the Pali word beside the English?
choices: English has no words for anything
The Pali is easier to spell
Each English word covers only part of the Pali meaning
check.why: Translations such as suffering for dukkha capture only part of the term.

review.q: Who were the first listeners of the first sermon, according to the texts?
choices: Five former companions of the Buddha
review.why: The sutta addresses the group of five monks who had fasted with Gotama.

review.q: Which translation of the first sermon is public domain and quoted in this chapter?
review.why: Rhys Davids' 1881 translation in Sacred Books of the East 11 is in the U.S. public domain.

review.q: What are the four noble truths about, in order?
choices: Suffering, its origin, its ending, the path
review.why: The sermon names suffering, its origin in craving, its cessation and the path.

review.q: What does the sutta say must be done with the truth of suffering?
choices: It is to be fully understood
review.why: Suffering is to be understood; craving abandoned; cessation realized; path developed.

review.q: Which listener does the sutta say understood first?

review.q: Why do scholars say the sutta repeats itself so much?
choices: It was kept by oral recitation
review.why: Repetition and lists supported memory in an oral tradition.

review.q: What does the Middle Way name in the first sermon?
choices: A road from Bodh Gaya to Sarnath
The path between pleasure-seeking and self-torment
review.why: The sermon opens by naming two extremes and a middle path between them.

review.q: Which statement describes the gods' cry without taking a side?
choices: The cry proves the sermon happened
The cry proves the sermon never happened
